title: Before I formed thee
author: Ruth Oduola
excerpt: Before your mother knew your name, God knew your days and your name. Before your first cell divided, a script was already written.
body: “Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee: and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.” — Jeremiah 1:5

Before your mother knew your name, God knew your days and your name. Before your first cell divided, before your heart learned to beat, long before your arrival on this earth, a script was already written; a life and a journey for you had been mapped out. The way you will navigate life, how you will bring pleasure to Him, the Author of Life had drafted it.

A story: your story, not a rough sketch, not a vague hope. A fully formed narrative, complete with His purpose, with your calling, with a unique pleasure only your life could bring to His heart had been written. Which explains that the very essence of you having the opportunity to see the light of this world is to bring pleasure to Him.
Now, the tragedy is that many live off-script, and the script remains waiting and unchanged. And the Author waits too, for the actors to return to the pages He wrote before time began.

God knows the ending from the beginning; He is all-knowing. Look at David. As a boy, barely a teenager, he tended sheep in lonely fields. No one saw a king, but God looked at that young boy and said, “I have found a man after My own heart.” Consider Joseph: he was very young when the Lord told him what his future would be. In between the dream and the fulfilment of his dream were the pit, Potiphar's house and the prison. God had shown him the final page, but Joseph had to walk through the chapters he would not have written for himself.

The thought He has for you is a good one, to bring you to an expected end. It is not only about God's willingness to bring you to an expected end; it is also about you following Him, and your willingness to trust Him through it all.

title: Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker
author: Ruth Oduola
excerpt: Have you seen a man who argues blindly with the writer of a movie on how the movie will turn out? That is how many of us argue with the Writer of our scripts.
body: Have you seen a man who argues blindly with the writer of a movie on how the movie will turn out? That's exactly the way many of us argue blindly with the Writer of our scripts. The Writer of the script knows the beginning, He knows what is next, each chapter, each scene, each act, even till the end.
“Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?” — Isaiah 45:9

Bring to remembrance Jacob, a good example of a man who strove with God and with man. Before his arrival at the house of Laban, God met with him, and he made a vow: “If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go… then shall the Lord be my God.” See the silent words of Jacob: “If You will be with me”, though God had just said, “I will be with you.” “In this way that I go”, not the way God had chosen, but the way Jacob himself had determined. This man was giving God the criteria to follow Him. He finished his vow by saying then, not now, shall the Lord be my God. A man procrastinating his allegiance to his Creator!

Are you struggling with God? Do you think your ways are better than His? No one has ever been at loggerheads with his Maker and rejoiced. To strive with the Potter is to be broken, not in the way of Peniel, which leads to blessing, but in the way of pride, which leads to destruction.

Dearly beloved, God knew you before you were formed. Why should you strive with your Maker on this journey you know little or nothing about? The best you know about yourself is only a glimpse of the full picture the Creator has drafted out for you to walk in. Surrender all, and let Him lead you on this journey of life.

title: Let no man despise thy youth
author: Ruth Oduola
excerpt: If life were a day, the teen years are the dawn. The gifts God placed inside you begin to wake up and whisper, “We are here.”
body: If life were a day, then the teen years are the dawn. This is when the sun begins to rise, and light breaks through, though darkness still lingers. It is in this season that the gifts God placed inside you begin to wake up. They start stirring, they begin to surface and they begin to ask for your attention. The very things that will shape your future start to whisper, “We are here.”

And yet, so many young people have no idea what God has placed inside them. They walk through their dawn as if it were still midnight, not knowing that the day has already begun. The choices made at that point determine the chances in the future. Zeal and passion are much in this stage, but wisdom is little.
“He looked David over and saw that he was only a boy, ruddy and handsome, and he despised him.” — 1 Samuel 17:42

When his mates were playing hide and seek, David was in the bush tending his father's sheep and seeking the Lord. He had grown up in the heart, though feeble in physical appearance. Saul despised him, Goliath despised him, his own brothers despised him, but David heeded the word of Scripture: “Let no man despise thy youth.” Many will aim to despise your youth; you are the one who will not allow it.

What are you using your today to do? Your time of manifestation should not be your time of preparation. Are you still afraid of drawing the sword, still afraid of starting what God has told you to start? “I need more time,” is what many keep saying, until time is no more. Beloved, grow up from being a teenager at heart, and start facing your Goliaths early in life.

title: The bright morning of life
author: Ruth Oduola
excerpt: The youthful years are the bright morning of life, when strength is abundant. Bear the burden while there is still strength.
body: Viewing life through the lens of a day, the youthful years are like the bright morning. Your strength is at its peak and your mind is sharp, ready to face the day. That is what the youthful years are meant to be: the season when strength is abundant and the day stretches out before you, full of promise.
“It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.” — Lamentations 3:27

Every man has a yoke to bear, and will at a stage in life bear it upon himself. However, if at the time of his strength he refuses to carry it, he will bear it when his strength begins to fail him. And a yoke carried in old age, without the youthful energy, is a heavier yoke.

After killing Goliath, David did not go straight to the throne. He spent his twenties in the wilderness, fleeing from Saul and living in caves. Yet he was in his bright morning: he gathered and trained the mighty men who later became his generals, fought battles, learned leadership and wrote psalms. When he finally became king at thirty, he was ready, because he had spent his bright morning preparing. Joshua, too, spent his young years serving Moses and learning leadership. Samson's story is the warning: his strength was legendary, but he squandered it, because he never fully surrendered it to God.

The strength of the young is not to be wasted; it is to be invested. What you do now determines what becomes of you later. Learn as much as you can, work as much as you can; however, remember that what is not of eternal value is eternally useless. Never make the mistake of saying, “I will serve God when I am much older.” Oh, youthful one, remember now your Creator in the days of thy youth.
“But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.” — Matthew 6:33. Bear the burden while there is still strength!

title: Where are you?
author: Ruth Oduola
excerpt: In a bid to find bread, have you exchanged your fire? God is asking: “Son, daughter, where are you? You are not where I placed you.”
body: If life is a day, then adulthood is the busiest part of it. A man leaves home early, and from the moment he arrives at work he is pulled in many directions: calls to make, meetings to attend, deadlines to meet. He looks at the clock; it is just past noon. He looks again, and suddenly it is evening. That is exactly what the adult years feel like: the hustling and bustling years of life.

During this stage of life, distractions are at their peak. The pressure to provide, to build, to achieve, to keep up is relentless. And here is the quiet danger: without realising it, a person can begin to exchange his faith for the search for daily bread. Prayer time is swallowed up by work time. Fellowship with other believers is replaced by networking with business associates. The things of God that once mattered begin to feel like things that can wait.

I hope that in a bid to find bread, you have not exchanged your fire. God is asking a question, and He is asking you directly: “Son, daughter, where are you? You are not where I placed you.” Like Jonah, who was called to Nineveh but boarded a ship to Tarshish, many have allowed the currents of this passing world to carry them far from the shores of purpose.
If you know, deep within, that you have drifted, then hear this: a turnaround is better than a wasted journey. Take a U-turn. Come back to where you ought to be. It is not too late.

Solomon had everything this world could offer, and when he looked back over all his hands had done, he wrote: “Behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.” Do not be like the servant who buried his one talent. Our Lord will soon come to ask for what He has given to each one. Will you be found a faithful steward?
